Auto-summary (auto-generated): Discussed POC scope around latency/throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), benchmark plan, and timeline; agreed to share sample traffic and run lab benchmarks next week.

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood, this is Mina our systems eng, we'll run through the poc scope focused on the latency and throughput SLOs you mentioned in the intake form
00:13 Alex: hey thanks, yea we're excited, priya and marcus are here to cover ml and infra, wanted to make sure we nail TTFT targets for interactive product and TPOT for bulk generation jobs
00:28 Mina: great, just to align on definitions - Jordan, do you want to run TTFT vs TPOT so we all use same language?
00:35 Jordan: sure - in our framing TTFT is time to first token, that's the latency users feel when they hit send; TPOT is time per token / time to produce tokens after the first, which maps to throughput and sustained latency; for SLOs we usually set p95 and p99 on TTFT for interactive flows and on TPOT for both interactive and batch depending on output length
01:02 Priya: ok that matches our intuition, but can you be concrete - what numbers are realistic for, say, 32 token responses vs 512 token summaries?
01:14 Mina: right, so short replies (<=32 tokens) we aim for TTFT p95 < 120ms and p99 < 250ms on dedicated stacks; for long outputs we care more about aggregate time — TPOT p95 ~ 10-25ms per token depending on model and quantization. so a 512 token summary at 20ms/token is ~10.2s total, those are ballpark
01:41 Marcus: 10s sounds long for some endpoints, but we don't need real-time for all flows. Our interactive chat must feel snappy — ideally p95 < 150ms TTFT and p99 < 300ms. We've seen other vendors promise <100ms but at high cost
02:01 Jordan: totally, it's a tradeoff. Also TTFT vs TPOT depends heavily on cache state and batching. Warm KV cache improves TTFT, and batching inflates TTFT for single requests but improves TPOT amortized across many requests
02:25 Alex: can you explain the measurement plan - how do we account for warm vs cold and realistic traffic? Sometimes lab runs look great but production tails are bad
02:36 Mina: good question. Our recommended plan: 1) Replay a representative production trace at multiple qps levels (we ask customer to provide sample CSV); 2) Synthetic microbench to measure cold-starts and kernel latencies (single request, no cache); 3) Hot run with warmed KV cache and realistic concurrency to measure steady-state TTFT/TPOT; 4) Tail sampling over 24-72h in a shadow/proxy mode to capture real production variability. We'll report p50/p95/p99 and also show token throughput (tokens/sec) and cost per 1M tokens
03:12 Priya: how many requests do you need for a reliable p99? We have some spiky traffic but overall only ~50k requests/day for the endpoint
03:22 Mina: statistically you'd want several thousand samples per latency bucket; for p99 a minimum of 10k samples gives more confidence but we can also use longer windows and combine runs. That's why we recommend a 24-72h shadow capture to get real tails
03:40 Jordan: also note we calculate p95/p99 on request-level TTFT, and for TPOT we do per-token latency histograms and aggregate to estimate completed time. We can surface both request tail and token tail.
03:56 Marcus: infra constraints: we prefer VPC/private deployment but for POC we can use dedicated hosted nodes if isolation is okay. Any differences in SLOs between hosted vs private?
04:10 Mina: performance is primarily config + hardware. Dedicated capacity in Redwood gives predictable throughput and lower tail latency. VPC/private adds networking hops which can add small jitter; we quantify network latency separately during bench. In our experience p95 adds ~10-30ms depending on peering
04:30 Alex: breakdown on observability: we need per-request traces, token-level timings, and KV cache hit rates. Do you provide that in the console?
04:40 Jordan: yes, Console shows token-level cost and latency, model-level dashboards, and you can export request traces. We'll include a sample dashboard in the benchmark report
04:49 Priya: about metrics - can you include TTFT split by prompt size and by context length? We have variable context windows up to 8k tokens
05:01 Mina: absolutely - we'll stratify the results by prompt length buckets (<=64, 65-512, >512) and by cache state. We'll also show per-sequence length throughput curves and recommended batch sizes/quantization profiles
05:18 Jordan: quick note on batch sizing: for interactive low-latency we recommend small batch sizes and concurrency knobs; for throughput-heavy jobs you can increase batching to improve tokens/sec with slight TTFT penalty
05:30 Alex: ok, what's the proposed SLO set we should validate in the POC?
05:38 Jordan: suggested POC SLOs: (1) TTFT interactive endpoint: p95 < 150ms, p99 < 300ms for <=64 token responses with warm cache; (2) TPOT sustained: p95 token latency < 25ms/token for typical model variant; (3) Bulk generation throughput: achieve >= 200 tokens/sec per GPU (example target depends on model/quant) for the chosen model; (4) Cold start baseline: single-request cold TTFT p95 < 500ms for quantized models on dedicated nodes
06:08 Priya: those seem reasonable as acceptance criteria, but we may set stricter TTFT for our primary chatflow later. For the POC let's use these as pass/fail thresholds
06:19 Marcus: what about concurrency and qps targets for the bench? we plan to run at peak 120 qps for the interactive endpoint and batch jobs of ~4 concurrent workers for bulk
06:29 Mina: ok we'll run a curve: 10, 50, 120, 250 qps for interactive to see where degradation starts. For bulk we'll test batch sizes and worker counts to find tokens/sec per GPU. We'll include resource utilization (GPU, CPU, mem) traces
06:46 Jordan: measurement specifics: we compute p95/p99 over 5-minute rolling windows and also show daily aggregates. For formal acceptance we recommend using the 95th/99th over a 6-hour steady-state window from the hot run
07:02 Alex: good. Also, any special handling for streaming responses? our chat uses streaming a lot and time to first byte matters a lot
07:12 Mina: streaming is effectively TTFT for the first chunk and then TPOT for the subsequent chunks. We'll measure first-chunk latency and median chunk frequency. There are some nuances with underlying protocol (http2 vs websockets) that affect observed metrics
07:30 Priya: model variants - we currently use a 13B model quantized to int8 in prod. Will you test the same or recommend a different variant for the POC?
07:40 Mina: we'll test your 13B int8 profile and a 7B and a 13B fp16 baseline to show tradeoffs. Part of Redwood Optimize suggestions will recommend quantization vs latency tradeoffs and the expected cost delta
07:55 Marcus: security and compliance - we need SOC2 and data retention terms before any shadow traffic. Can you send that?
08:03 Jordan: yes, we'll share SOC2 report and security docs; for POC we can sign a short NDA and enable audit logs. We'll add the security contact to next steps
08:15 Alex: timeline? how long to get meaningful numbers?
08:19 Jordan: propose: week 0 (this week) - kickoff and data collection, week 1 - lab benchmark (synthetic + replay) and initial results, week 2 - shadow run / extended capture and tuning, week 3 - final report and decision. So ~2-3 weeks total
08:41 Priya: do you need any infra changes from our side? request routing, tokens, VPC peering?
08:47 Marcus: we can open peering and provide a sample traffic CSV. We'll need a security contact for the SOC2 exchange
08:55 Jordan: perfect. Bench details we'll run: - baseline microbench: single-threaded cold TTFT for model variants - replay bench: sample trace replayed at 10/50/120/250 qps for 60-90s each - steady-state hot bench: warmed KV, run 2hr capture for p95/p99 stability - bulk bench: measure tokens/sec at different batch sizes and worker counts - network latency experiments: measure peered vs public path
09:25 Priya: will you provide the runner or do we run the scripts?
09:28 Mina: we provide both. Redwood will run lab benchmarks and share scripts/terraform you can run in your VPC for private tests. For shadow we'll provide a lightweight proxy shim to capture traces safely
09:41 Alex: good, cost implications - can you give rough delta between hosted best-effort vs dedicated?
09:45 Jordan: rough guidance: dedicated capacity reduces tail and gives predictable cost; hosted pay-as-you-go is cheaper initially but can have variable tails at scale. We'll include estimated cost per 1M tokens for the proposed config in the quote
09:58 Marcus: any recommended observability SLOs beyond p95/p99? e.g., error rate thresholds, retry behaviors
10:04 Mina: we'll include error-rate targets (<=0.1% request errors), retry budgets, and recommended fallback policies (model variant fallback, regional fallback). We'll also propose tracing hooks for debugging spikes
10:18 Alex: ok let's recap next steps verbally
10:21 Jordan: recap - Redwood sends benchmark plan, scripts, SOC2 and security docs; Ember shares sample traffic CSV, primary security contact, and infra constraints; schedule lab run for 2026-09-22; both teams align on acceptance SLOs (TTFT p95<150ms etc).
10:41 Priya: agreed
10:43 Marcus: agreed, will share CSV by Friday
10:45 Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the benchmark plan.
